reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods
chapter_title: Assessment and Acceptance of Drilled Shafts

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Final step of a drilled shaft project: official acceptance of as-built shafts by the engineer in responsible charge. Acceptance requires complete installation records and demonstration that shaft conforms to Plans and Specifications including post-construction integrity testing. Imperfections are to be expected; a robust design should be tolerant of small unavoidable flaws. An imperfection requires remediation when the shaft is insufficient to meet strength and serviceability requirements during design life. Key terms: anomaly — deviation from norm; often detected by NDT, may or may not be a defect; flaw — deviation from planned shape or material characteristics; defect — flaw that may significantly detract from drilled shaft performance (ASTM D6760); deficient — insufficient or inadequate; remediation — correcting a fault or deficiency; repair — restore to condition meeting performance requirements.
key_points: Acceptance requires complete installation records + NDT results + conformance with Plans and Specs
Anomaly → Flaw → Defect: increasing severity per ASTM D6760 terminology
Defect requires remediation only if shaft is deficient (insufficient to meet performance requirements)
Perfection is unattainable; robust design tolerates small unavoidable flaws
sections.applicability: Post-construction quality assurance; acceptance decision framework for all drilled shafts

sections.title: Assessment of Completed Drilled Shafts
sections.body: Two categories of information for acceptance: (1) field observations during construction (inspection records per Chapter 15); (2) NDT results (CSL, TIP, GGL per Chapter 16). Process (Figure 17-1): review inspection records → review NDT results → accept or reject → if anomalies, engineering evaluation → accept as-is or remediate. Inspection records review: check casing, excavation log, slurry properties, base cleanout, cage inspection, concrete testing, volume monitoring; foundation design engineer is responsible for timely review. NDT recommendation: require NDT for ALL drilled shafts constructed using wet methods (slurry or water); also for all load test and technique shafts; consider also for dry construction with challenging conditions (congested cage, excavation stability concerns). NDT anomaly classification per Table 17-1: Class A (acceptable) — CSL FAT increase <15%, energy reduction <9 dB; TIP radius reduction Rr <6%, local cover >3 in.; GGL <3 standard deviations below mean. Class B (conditionally acceptable) — CSL per Table 16-2 intermediate values. Class C (abnormal) — CSL FAT increase per Table 16-2; TIP Rr >6% or local cover <3 in.; GGL >3 SD below mean. Decision process: Class A = accept; Class B = review records, may require additional action; Class C = further evaluation required (CT tomography, coring, additional testing).
key_points: Require NDT on ALL wet-method shafts; all load test and technique shafts
Class A: acceptable — no action required
Class B: conditionally acceptable — review records; may need further action
Class C: abnormal — further evaluation required (CSL tomography, coring)
Foundation design engineer responsible for timely review of inspection records and NDT

sections.title: Types of Deficiencies in Completed Shafts
sections.body: Geotechnical strength or serviceability deficiencies: insufficient shaft length to mobilize required resistance; poor quality bearing material at tip; loosening of soil around shaft due to caving or poor construction; excessive settlement due to inadequate consolidation of bearing material after improper base cleanout. Structural deficiencies: zones of weak or absent concrete (necking, void, soil inclusion); discontinuity in reinforcement; insufficient cover; geometric defects (misalignment exceeding tolerance). Common causes of structural defects: concrete flow blocked by rebar or debris; slurry contamination of concrete; loss of slurry head during concrete placement; premature casing extraction; caving during excavation; separation of tremie from concrete; tremie joints failure. During construction incidents that may be addressed before completion: sidewall sloughing (restore stability); loosening of ground (change methods, adjust diameter/length); inflow of water in dry hole (flood and use wet methods); tremie problems (stop, remove fluid concrete before set, restart after re-excavating).
key_points: Geotechnical deficiencies: insufficient length, poor bearing material, loose soil, excessive settlement
Structural deficiencies: weak concrete zones, necking, voids, soil inclusions, discontinuous reinforcement
Tremie problems may allow re-excavation and restart if concrete is still fluid
Document all incidents; communicate to design engineer promptly for decisions
sections.applicability: Deficiency identification; pre- and post-completion problem classification

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.body: Engineering evaluation process when defect is identified: (1) determine location and extent of defect from NDT, coring, video, construction records; (2) classify defect type (structural vs. geotechnical) and assess severity; (3) determine whether defect causes shaft to be deficient (fails to meet design requirements); (4) if not deficient, document rationale and accept; (5) if deficient, develop remediation plan. Engineering judgment for Class C NDT results: coring is not automatically required; for small anomalies in non-critical locations, engineer may accept with documented rationale. If coring performed and finds competent concrete with acceptable strength: accept (document number and locations of cores taken). If coring finds defective concrete: proceed to engineering evaluation of impact on performance and develop remediation plan.
key_points: Evaluation steps: locate defect → classify → assess whether deficient → accept or remediate
Coring not automatically required for Class C NDT results; engineering judgment required
Accept with documented rationale when defect location/extent does not render shaft deficient
Only one core boring: consider additional borings to verify no significant defect was missed
sections.applicability: Engineering evaluation of detected anomalies and defects

sections.title: Remediation Methods
sections.body: Ground improvement: improve soil resistance around deficient shaft using grouting, jet grouting, or other ground improvement methods to increase side or base resistance. Supplemental foundations and/or structural bridging: install additional drilled shafts, micropiles, or other foundations adjacent to deficient shaft; install structural cap or beam to bridge load from deficient shaft to adjacent foundations. Excavation and replacement: excavate deficient shaft and replace with new shaft; applicable when shaft is relatively shallow or defect is near top; avoid for deep shafts or shafts already incorporated into structure above. Structural enhancement: add reinforcement, jacketing, or other structural elements to strengthen deficient zone in shaft; may involve coring, cleaning, injecting epoxy or grout into defect zone. Grouting: pressure grouting to fill voids or strengthen weak concrete; sleeve-port tube grouting along shaft sides; post-grouting through tubes preinstalled at shaft base (Appendix H) for base resistance enhancement. Case histories: examples in Chapter 17 illustrate successful remediation of various defect types.
key_points: Ground improvement: increase side/base resistance around deficient shaft
Supplemental foundations: additional drilled shafts or micropiles adjacent; structural cap to bridge
Excavation and replacement: applicable for shallow shafts; avoid for deep or already-integrated shafts
Structural enhancement: epoxy or grout injection into defect zone; jacketing
Grouting: post-grouting for base resistance; sleeve-port tubes for side; pressure grouting for voids
sections.applicability: Remediation of deficient drilled shafts after construction
